To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the total cross sections of sphere clusters can differ greatly from the sum of isolated-sphere cross section, (2) a dipole representation is inadequate for the prediction of the cross section of highly conducting sphere clusters, (3) the cross section of sphere clusters is a strong function of cluster geometry, and (4) the cross section is a strong function, in the near field, of the size parameter of the constituent spheres.

(a) the absorption cross section for a pair of spheres is greater than the sum of the individual sphere cross sections; (b) for highly conducting spheres, several multipole orders must be included in the expansion to obtain accurate cross sections; (c) the extinction, scattering, and absorption cross sections of clusters can be calculated analytically; (d) the scattering cross section of a fractal cluster of small spheres is greater than that of the same number of isolated spheres; (e)

(1) a method is developed for calculating the orientation-averages extinction, absorption, scattering cross sections of sphere clusters; (2) a dipole representation does not adequately predict absorption cross section of small spheres; (3) absorption of sphere clusters is significantly greater than that of individual spheres.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a method for calculating the total cross sections of sphere clusters, which is applicable to clusters of spheres of any size and material properties.
the scattering of electromagnetic waves by a collection of small particles in random positions.
the calculation of the optical properties of clusters of neighboring spherical scatterers for fixed and random orientations of the spheres.
